title: The inverse trade-off between Alpha and Beta at fixed sample size
scenario_markdown: A semiconductor manufacturing fabrication facility tests wafer electrical resistance to ensure process stability ($H_0: \mu = 50\ \Omega$ vs $H_1: \mu \ne 50\ \Omega$). To reduce false alarms that unnecessarily halt the cleanroom production line, process engineering reduces the test significance level from $\alpha = 0.05$ to $\alpha = 0.01$, while holding the sample size strictly fixed at $n = 50$ wafers per shift.

parameters.objective: Understand why lowering alpha increases beta and why increasing n reduces both

assumptions: Underlying process variation sigma is stable
A specific alternative value mu_1 != 50 is evaluated for power

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual relationship between alpha and beta. For a fixed sample size, lowering alpha pushes the critical value outward, expanding the non-rejection region and inevitably increasing beta (reducing power). The only way to lower both error rates simultaneously is to increase sample size n.

stages.prompt_markdown: What happens to the probability of a Type II error ($\beta$) and the statistical power of the test ($1 - \beta$) as a direct consequence of lowering $\alpha$ from $0.05$ to $0.01$ with sample size fixed at $n = 50$?

options.text_markdown: Both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ decrease because a smaller significance level makes the test more rigorous overall.
options.hint_markdown: Lowering $\alpha$ demands stronger evidence to reject $H_0$, which increases the probability of failing to reject a false null (raising $\beta$).

options.text_markdown: $\beta$ remains completely unchanged because $\beta$ depends solely on sample size $n$, not on $\alpha$.
options.hint_markdown: The critical cutoff that separates rejection from non-rejection is directly dictated by $\alpha$; moving this boundary directly alters the area under the alternative distribution ($\beta$).
Power is $1 - \beta$. As $\beta$ rises when $\alpha$ is lowered, power falls.

stages.explanation_markdown: For a fixed sample size $n$, there is an inescapable inverse trade-off between $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Decreasing $\alpha$ from $0.05$ to $0.01$ moves the critical values further into the tails, widening the "Fail to reject $H_0$" region. While this reduces false alarms (Type I errors), it makes it harder to detect true shifts away from $50\ \Omega$, thereby increasing $\beta$ (Type II error) and lowering test power ($1 - \beta$).

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the only method by which process engineers can reduce both Type I error probability ($\alpha$) and Type II error probability ($\beta$) at the same time?

options.text_markdown: Increase the sample size $n$, which shrinks standard error and reduces overlap between the null and alternative sampling distributions.
Switch the test from a two-tailed test to a one-tailed test without gathering additional data.
options.hint_markdown: Switching tails alters directionality and tail area, but does not provide extra information or overcome the fundamental error trade-off.

options.text_markdown: Use the standard normal $z$-distribution instead of the $t$-distribution.
options.hint_markdown: Changing the reference distribution without changing underlying sampling variance cannot reduce both errors simultaneously.
The $p$-value is an outcome calculated from observed sample data, not a tunable engineering parameter.

stages.explanation_markdown: The only way to achieve a "free lunch" in statistical testing—reducing $\alpha$ and $\beta$ simultaneously—is to collect more data (increase $n$). A larger sample size compresses the standard error ($SE = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$), pulling the sampling distributions under $H_0$ and $H_1$ further apart so that their overlapping error regions both shrink.
